name: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
title: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
answer: Keeping financial data out of public models covers the controls that stop ledgers, payroll files, deal documents and client records from being pasted into consumer chatbots or uploaded to third party AI services. It sits inside the wider governance and risk work of an accounting function, alongside data protection, confidentiality and professional ethics duties. The concern is not only deliberate misuse, since staff often paste a spreadsheet into a chat window to get a quick summary or formula. Scope therefore includes the tools staff may use, the data they may touch and the review of any AI vendor that processes firm or client information.

Governance, Risk and Financial Data Security

sections.body: Keeping financial data out of public models covers the controls that stop ledgers, payroll files, deal documents and client records from being pasted into consumer chatbots or uploaded to third party AI services. It sits inside the wider governance and risk work of an accounting function, alongside data protection, confidentiality and professional ethics duties. The concern is not only deliberate misuse, since staff often paste a spreadsheet into a chat window to get a quick summary or formula. Scope therefore includes the tools staff may use, the data they may touch and the review of any AI vendor that processes firm or client information.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The practical setup is a mix of network controls, identity management and approved tooling. Many firms block consumer AI domains at the firewall or proxy, log attempts and route permitted requests through an enterprise tenant with no training on submitted data. Data loss prevention rules flag account numbers, tax identifiers and large numeric tables leaving the estate, while device management limits local AI apps. Where a firm runs its own models, the data stays inside its cloud tenancy or on premises, and access follows the same role based controls as the finance systems themselves.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with a data map that marks which systems hold client confidential, personal or market sensitive information and who can reach them. From that map a firm sets tiers, for example open public data, internal only and restricted client data, and states which AI services each tier may touch. Approved tools are tested and documented, prompts and outputs are logged where feasible, and vendor terms are checked for retention, training and subprocessor clauses. Staff get short, specific guidance with examples from their own workflows, and the control is tested through spot checks rather than assumed to work.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Accountants already carry confidentiality and professional conduct obligations, and data protection law adds duties on lawful basis, retention and cross border transfer. A public model that retains prompts can turn a routine query into a disclosure, and the firm may not learn about it until a client or regulator asks. Ownership of the data, the model output and any derived work should be settled in vendor contracts, with breach notification timelines and audit rights. Records of what was submitted, by whom and under which approval are the evidence base if a complaint or an investigation follows.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect tighter vendor terms, more enterprise deployments that contractually exclude training on customer data and growing use of private or locally hosted models for sensitive work. Regulators are paying closer attention to AI use in financial reporting and advice, and audit teams are starting to ask how client data was handled during engagements. The direction is toward fewer blanket bans and more graded access, with clear approval paths so staff can use useful tools without exposing the numbers that matter.
